cases.abstract: A larger context window does not establish that a language model can use evidence wherever it appears. We test this distinction through multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, changing context length and evidence position while preserving the required answer. Across the evaluated models, question-answering accuracy generally peaks at the beginning or end of the context and falls when the answer-bearing passage moves to the middle; in some GPT-3.5-Turbo settings, supplied evidence yields lower accuracy than answering without documents. Extended-context versions show little advantage when the input fits both versions' windows. Several models also struggle with middle-position UUID pairs, although both evaluated Claude variants retrieve them nearly perfectly. Repeating the query before and after the data largely eliminates synthetic retrieval errors but leaves the question-answering pattern substantially unchanged. In an open-domain question-answering case study, reader accuracy saturates while retrieval recall continues to improve. Together, these comparisons distinguish input capacity from effective evidence use: neither a larger window, additional retrieved documents, nor improved exact matching necessarily translates into better contextual question answering.
cases.methods: To test whether models use evidence independently of its location, we relocate the answer-bearing paragraph while holding the question, document set, and required answer fixed. For 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with paragraph annotations, contexts contain that paragraph and retrieved Wikipedia distractors excluding annotated answers. Reordering tests position at a fixed length; varying the total from 10 to 20 or 30 documents tests the effect of additional distractors. Closed-book prompts measure accuracy without supplied evidence, and oracle prompts with only the answer paragraph provide a reference without distractor competition. Synthetic retrieval replaces documents with serialized JSON containing random UUID keys and values, reducing linguistic confounders while retaining the need to locate one relevant item. We vary its position across 75, 140, or 300 pairs, using 500 examples per setting. With greedy decoding, both tasks score whether a correct answer or value appears in the output.
cases.results: Query placement distinguishes successful token matching from successful use of evidence. With 300 UUID key-value pairs, placing the query before and after the data gives GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) perfect retrieval accuracy, compared with a worst-case accuracy of 45.6% without that intervention. In multi-document question answering, however, the same prompt change slightly improves accuracy when evidence comes first and slightly decreases it elsewhere, leaving the positional pattern substantially intact. Making the query available during context processing therefore helps this synthetic lookup task without resolving the observed difficulty with natural-language evidence. Training length further changes the interpretation: Flan-UL2 has only a 1.9-percentage-point spread across evidence positions within its 2,048-token training window, but develops a middle-position disadvantage on longer inputs. GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K counterpart also have nearly overlapping accuracy curves on the 10- and 20-document inputs that fit both windows. These comparisons make task demands and training context relevant to evaluating long-context capability, rather than treating nominal window size as sufficient.
cases.notes: Retained the distinction between input capacity and evidence use, with query-placement results as the discriminating comparison (Sections 3-4). Section 2 supports the closed-book adverse finding and shared-window comparison; Section 5 supports saturation before retrieval recall. The 45.6% value is a worst-case retrieval accuracy, not an average. Claude is an exception on synthetic retrieval, and Flan-UL2's small positional spread holds within its training window. Architectural explanations remain hypotheses.

cases.abstract: Retrieved passages can improve factual answers without ensuring that generated claims are supported by the passages cited. Self-RAG addresses this mismatch by training a language model to encode retrieval decisions, passage relevance, evidential support, and response utility in reflection tokens generated alongside response text. A separately trained critic supplies annotations offline; at inference, the generator evaluates its own passage-conditioned continuations and ranks them using generation probabilities and critique scores. This makes predicted evidence support part of sentence selection, with adjustable priorities rather than a fixed retrieve-and-generate pipeline. Zero-shot evaluations of trained 7B and 13B models cover factual question answering, classification, biographies, and cited long-form answers. Against a 7B model trained on the same instruction-output pairs but augmented with retrieval only at test time, Self-RAG improves long-tail PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9%. On ASQA, its citation precision exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT, while citation recall and answer correctness remain lower. Increasing the support weight improves precision but reduces measured fluency. The results support controllable evidence use while showing that better attribution need not improve every dimension of answer quality.
cases.methods: Self-RAG selects among sentences conditioned on different retrieved passages, using predicted evidence support as a decoding criterion. A Llama 2-7B critic trained on GPT-4 feedback annotates instruction-output pairs with retrieval decisions and judgments of relevance, support, and utility. The generator learns response text and these reflection tokens together through next-token prediction, with retrieved passages excluded from the training loss. At inference, a normalized retrieval-token probability is compared with a threshold. If retrieval is triggered, the generator produces separate candidate sentences from different passages, then combines each candidate's generation probability with weighted probabilities of favorable critique tokens. Segment-level beam search retains the highest-scoring continuations. This lets predicted support influence which claims enter the answer and allows the relevance, support, and utility priorities to change without retraining. The critic provides offline supervision rather than additional inference-time evaluations.
cases.results: A baseline trained on the same instruction-output pairs does not reproduce Self-RAG's attribution gains. Llama2-FT7B is trained on those pairs without passages or reflection tokens and receives retrieval only at test time. Self-RAG 7B raises long-tail PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9% and ASQA citation precision from 5.0% to 66.9%, yet ASQA correctness (str-em) falls from 31.0% to 30.0%. The combination therefore improves attribution without uniformly improving answer content. On the same five ASQA input documents, Self-RAG 13B exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT in citation precision, 70.3% versus 65.1%, but trails in recall, 71.3% versus 76.6%, and answer correctness. Its stronger precision does not establish broader evidence coverage. The inference controls expose the same need to choose an objective: raising the support weight improves citation precision while lowering MAUVE, the reported fluency measure. Reducing retrieval frequency also harms PopQA accuracy more than PubHealth accuracy. Thus, the value of selective retrieval and critique depends on both the task and the aspect of output quality being prioritized.
cases.notes: Retained both evidence-attribution gains and inference-time control. Table 2 supports the same-pair comparison and the adverse ASQA correctness and recall findings; Figure 3 supports the precision-fluency and retrieval-frequency trade-offs. Shared instruction-output pairs do not mean identical training procedures. Main models use 150k pairs; 50k-pair ablations and the 150-instance ASQA ablation subset are separate evaluations. Reflection scores are learned judgments, not support certificates.
